summary.text: The defining sum satisfies \(a_{n+1}=(2^n-1)a_n+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\); for odd \(p\), Fermat’s theorem and the fact that shifting \(n\) by \(2(p-1)\) changes the triangular exponent by a multiple of \(p-1\) make both the coefficient and inhomogeneous term periodic, so induction from \(a_1=1\) proves the claim. For \(p=2\), the same recurrence shows directly that every \(a_n\) with \(n\ge1\) is odd.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_k=\binom{k+1}{2}=\frac{k(k+1)}2
\]
and, for \(n\geq 1\), define
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T_k}\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
(As usual, a product over an empty index set is \(1\).) We prove that for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a(n+2(p-1))\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

First derive a recurrence for \(a(n)\). In the defining sum for \(a(n+1)\), consider first an index \(k<n\). Its product is
\[
\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}(2^j-1)
=(2^n-1)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
Thus all terms with \(k<n\), when summed, contribute \((2^n-1)a(n)\). The one remaining term, corresponding to \(k=n\), has an empty product and is therefore \(2^{T_n}\). Consequently, for every \(n\geq 0\),
\[
\boxed{a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}.}\tag{1}
\]
Also, directly from the defining sum,
\[
a(1)=2^{T_0}=1.\tag{2}
\]

We first handle odd primes. Let \(p\) be an odd prime and put
\[
q=p-1,\qquad r=2q=2(p-1).
\]
Since \(p\neq 2\), the residue class of \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(p\). Fermat's little theorem therefore gives
\[
2^q=2^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p.\tag{3}
\]
It follows more generally that, for all nonnegative integers \(x,m\),
\[
2^{x+qm}=2^x(2^q)^m\equiv 2^x\pmod p.\tag{4}
\]

We now show that both pieces appearing in recurrence (1) are unchanged modulo \(p\) when its index is shifted by \(r\). For the coefficient, since \(r=2q\), equation (4) gives
\[
2^{n+r}=2^{n+2q}\equiv 2^n\pmod p,
\]
and hence
\[
2^{n+r}-1\equiv 2^n-1\pmod p.\tag{5}
\]

For the inhomogeneous term, we need the corresponding identity for triangular exponents. For arbitrary nonnegative integers \(n,q\), direct expansion gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{n+2q}-T_n
&=\binom{n+2q+1}{2}-\binom{n+1}{2}\\
&=\frac{(n+2q)(n+2q+1)-n(n+1)}2\\
&=q(2n+2q+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{T_{n+2q}=T_n+q(2n+2q+1).}\tag{6}
\]
In our situation \(q=p-1\), so the difference in (6) is a multiple of \(p-1\). Applying (4) yields
\[
2^{T_{n+r}}=2^{T_{n+2q}}\equiv 2^{T_n}\pmod p.\tag{7}
\]
Thus the coefficient and inhomogeneous term of recurrence (1) both repeat modulo \(p\) after \(r=2(p-1)\) steps.

It remains to prove that the solutions themselves agree after this shift. We establish by induction on \(n\geq 1\) that
\[
a(n+r)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.\tag{8}
\]
The initial case \(n=1\) requires some care because recurrence (1) relates \(a(r+1)\) to \(a(r)\), for which no periodicity assertion has yet been established. Apply (1) with index \(r=2q\):
\[
a(r+1)=(2^r-1)a(r)+2^{T_r}.
\]
By (3),
\[
2^r=2^{2q}=(2^q)^2\equiv 1\pmod p,
\]
so the coefficient \(2^r-1\) is \(0\) modulo \(p\). Moreover, formula (6) with \(n=0\) gives
\[
T_r=T_{2q}=T_0+q(2q+1)=q(2q+1),
\]
because \(T_0=0\). This exponent is a multiple of \(q=p-1\), and hence by (3)
\[
2^{T_r}=(2^q)^{2q+1}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(r+1)\equiv 0\cdot a(r)+1\equiv 1\equiv a(1)\pmod p,
\]
where the last equality uses (2). This proves the base case of (8).

Now suppose \(n\geq 1\) and
\[
a(n+r)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]
Using recurrence (1) at the indices \(n+r\) and \(n\), respectively, we have
\[
a(n+r+1)=(2^{n+r}-1)a(n+r)+2^{T_{n+r}}
\]
and
\[
a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}.
\]
The induction hypothesis identifies the two \(a\)-factors modulo \(p\), equation (5) identifies their coefficients, and equation (7) identifies the inhomogeneous terms. It follows that
\[
a(n+r+1)\equiv a(n+1)\pmod p.
\]
This completes the induction and proves (8) for every \(n\geq 1\) when \(p\) is odd.

It remains to treat the prime \(p=2\). We show first that
\[
a(n)\equiv 1\pmod 2\qquad(n\geq 1).\tag{9}
\]
The case \(n=1\) follows from \(a(1)=1\). Suppose \(n\geq 1\) and \(a(n)\equiv 1\pmod 2\). In recurrence (1), \(2^n\equiv 0\pmod 2\), so
\[
2^n-1\equiv -1\equiv 1\pmod 2.
\]
Also
\[
T_n=\binom{n+1}{2}=\frac{n(n+1)}2>0
\]
for \(n\geq 1\). Hence \(2^{T_n}\equiv 0\pmod 2\). Reducing (1) modulo \(2\) therefore gives
\[
a(n+1)\equiv 1\cdot a(n)+0\equiv 1\pmod 2.
\]
By induction, (9) holds for all \(n\geq 1\).

For \(p=2\), the proposed shift is
\[
2(p-1)=2.
\]
Both \(n\) and \(n+2\) are at least \(1\), so (9) immediately yields
\[
a(n+2)\equiv 1\equiv a(n)\pmod 2.
\]

Combining the odd-prime argument with the case \(p=2\), we conclude that for every prime \(p\) and every integer \(n\geq 1\),
\[
\boxed{a(n+2(p-1))\equiv a(n)\pmod p.}
\]
Equivalently, the remainders of these two integers upon division by \(p\) are equal, as required.
